name: Declarative Scalar Recalibration

1.definition: Can introduce a comparison that shifts the operative standard on a scale
1.details: The surface form attributes a belief to the addressee, but the constructional meaning is scalar recalibration: the speaker has Z that exceeds X on the Y dimension. Direction is flexible - the speaker may exceed from superiority (dismissive) or from being worse off (self-deprecating, ironic). Typically followed by the speaker's evidence for exceeding.

examples.form: [You think you're upset]. I wrote a paper predicting that this wouldn't happen.
examples.note: Self-deprecating; speaker exceeds on upset-scale due to embarrassing wrong prediction (Joshua Gans)

examples.form: [You think you're tired]? I've been up for 36 hours.
examples.note: With declarative-question construction layered; speaker exceeds on tiredness scale

examples.form: [You think that's expensive]. Wait till you see the repair bill.
examples.note: With demonstrative subject; introduces something more expensive

examples.form: [You think you know stress]. Try raising triplets.

constraints.description: Matrix clause with 2nd person subject and "think" as main verb
Requires follow-up providing speaker's evidence for exceeding on the scale

relatedConstructions.notes: The scalar-recalibration frame retains declarative clause type
Question prosody commonly layers onto the declarative scalar frame
Shares addressee-directed scalar-challenge function; differs in matrix verb and targets category membership rather than degree

grounds.locator: Ch. 13 §3, metalinguistic comparison; Ch. 16 §3.2, proposition assessment, for comparison

projection.target: You think that is loud can introduce an instance that shifts the operative degree standard. In a literal conversation about the hearer’s beliefs, the same sentence need not introduce a higher degree. The comparison depends on the following discourse.
projection.evidence: The source provides related scale and proposition-assessment analyses. The paired contexts illustrate the proposal and do not determine whether the reading has conventionalized.

curious.title: Topping someone's claim with your own
curious.summary: You think you're tired? can set up a comparison in which the speaker's own case goes further on the same scale.
curious.body: You think you're tired? I've been up for 36 hours. The first part looks like a remark about what you believe, but it can shift the scale. The speaker can be saying they're beyond tired, in a way that makes the listener's tiredness look smaller. Whether the sentence really works this way depends on what follows. A follow-up that gives the speaker's evidence, such as the 36 hours, supplies the comparison. In a literal conversation about what someone believes, the same sentence need not do this. This dictionary marks the analysis as provisional.

examples.text: [You think you're tired]? I've been up for 36 hours.
[You think that's expensive]. Wait till you see the repair bill.
[You think you know stress]. Try raising triplets.

curious.try: Think of a time someone said they were really tired, cold or busy. How would you top that with You think ...?

teacher.summary: Helps explain a belief-sounding frame that can top the listener's point on a scale.
teacher.explain: The frame You think you're/NP is [GRADABLE-PRED] has a matrix clause with a second person subject and think as the main verb, and the embedded predicate must be gradable. Its meaning can be scalar recalibration: the speaker has something that exceeds the addressee's example on the relevant dimension. The direction is flexible, since the speaker may exceed from superiority (dismissive) or from being worse off (self-deprecating, ironic). The pattern needs a follow-up giving the speaker's evidence. The comparison depends on the following discourse. This dictionary marks the analysis as provisional.
teacher.terms: In this dictionary it overlaps in function with a related scalar-challenge construction that has a different matrix verb and targets category membership rather than degree.

examples.text: [You think you're tired]? I've been up for 36 hours.
[You think that's expensive]. Wait till you see the repair bill.
[You think you know stress]. Try raising triplets.

watch_for: A learner might hear You think you're tired? only as a remark about the listener's belief, when a follow-up can show the speaker is topping it.
A learner might use the frame without a follow-up that supplies the speaker's own, bigger case.
teacher.activity: Students write a complaint about a mild condition (tired, cold, busy), pass it on, and the partner replies with You think ...? and an exaggerated case that tops it.

child.hook: What do you say when you've got it even worse than your friend?
child.explain: You think you're tired? can sound like a question about what you think. Sometimes it means "I'm even more tired." What the speaker says next shows which.

examples.text: [You think you're tired]? I've been up for 36 hours.
[You think that's expensive]. Wait till you see the repair bill.

child.play: Take turns. One person says "I'm tired" or "I'm cold". The other answers You think ...? and tops it with a reason.
